turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

That sounds incredibly stressful, and honestly, I don't envy the position you're in. There is so much weight attached to that name—nineteen years is a lifetime in this industry, and he commands a respect that a title like "Engineering Manager" doesn't automatically grant you.

When a director says "handle," it feels like a loaded gun, doesn't it? But you can't walk in there and just start swinging it. Not with him. If you come down on him like a typical performance review, you risk looking like the new kid who doesn't respect the elders, and he might just shut down out of pride.

Does he know the releases slipped because of him? Usually, guys with that much tenure are painfully aware of their own code. I wonder if there’s a way to frame this as you asking for his help to save the team’s reputation, rather than you disciplining him. If you approach it with "We have a problem, and I need your experience to solve it," you might get a different reaction than "You are the problem." How do you think he’d react to that?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Oh, wow. That changes everything. That isn't just a performance review; that feels like sitting down to tell your father he’s disappointing you.

Showing Suresh-ji a slide of defect metrics feels almost sacrilegious, doesn't it? It ignores everything he’s been for you and for this company. If you walk in there with corporate armor on—slides and metrics and HR speak—he’s going to feel more betrayed by the delivery than the message.

He knows he’s the reason for the slips. He has to. And he’s probably waiting for the axe to fall, maybe even wondering why you haven't come to him yet. You can't be his "manager" in that room. You have to be the daughter he spoke about at Diwali. You have to put the slides away, look him in the eye, and ask him what's going on. Because if you don't, you're just another boss to him, and that would be the biggest tragedy of all.

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I wish I could just say "yes." I really do, because I know you want a map to get out of this anxiety. But if I say yes, and you walk in there with a slide deck of defect metrics, I honestly think you might break something between you two that can’t be fixed.

The books are right about the *what*—you can’t hide the truth, and you can’t protect him from reality. But they are dead wrong about the *how* for Suresh-ji. "Radical candor" with a 56-year-old mentor who treats you like daughter doesn't look like a performance review; it looks like a difficult conversation between family.

If you walk in there "professional and kind" with a slide deck, he won't see a manager. He’ll see the girl he made chai for turning into a corporate robot. It will hurt him.

So, no. Don't bring the slides. Be direct about the problem—yes, absolutely. But do it as *you*, the person he respects, not the manager the books told you to be. Can you try telling him the hard truth without the props?

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

That fear—that you are the villain no matter what path you take—is the real tax on being a manager, and it hurts. It feels like there is no way to be a good daughter *and* a good leader at the same time.

But here is the thing about letting him coast. If you move his module or hide the metrics to protect him, you aren't treating him like a peer or a mentor. You are treating him like a liability. You are deciding, without his input, that he is done. That is a quiet kind of cruelty that might actually hurt his pride more than the truth.

The version where you aren't the villain isn't the one where you save him from reality. It's the one where you give him the dignity of the truth.

Even if it ends in a PIP, or a parting of ways, if you look him in the eye and treat him like an adult who deserves honesty rather than a child who needs protecting, you aren't the villain. You're the person who respected him enough to tell him the truth. The "villain" is the situation, not you. You're just the one brave enough to stand in the middle of it.
